vignette:
Marcus

Marcus is a fifty-three-year-old photographer of Samoan descent who sits in the therapy office with his shoulders drawn inward, as though he's still trying to make himself smaller. His weathered hands-the hands that once held cameras with steady confidence-rest in his lap, occasionally clenching into fists before he consciously uncurls them.

Seven years ago, Marcus was on assignment in Southeast Asia, documenting the lives of fishing communities for a major magazine. He was traveling alone, something he'd done dozens of times before without incident. On his way back to his hotel one evening, he was abducted at gunpoint by men involved in human trafficking. What was meant to be a three-week assignment became a nightmare that lasted forty-three days.

He doesn't speak much about those specific weeks. He mentions being held in a compound, the uncertainty of whether he would be killed, the constant noise and chaos, the loss of any sense of control over his own body and time. What he does talk about is the aftermath-the part that never seems to end.

When Marcus was finally rescued by authorities, he returned to his wife, Catherine, physically intact but fundamentally altered. In the first year, he tried to resume his work. He'd return to his studio, set up his equipment, and find himself paralyzed-unable to frame a shot, unable to make decisions about light and composition. The act of looking through a lens felt like an invasion of privacy, even when photographing inanimate objects. He eventually stopped trying.

Now, Marcus spends most of his days at home. He wakes at three or four in the morning, his body jolting awake with a racing heart and the sensation of being trapped in a confined space, even though he's in his own bed with Catherine beside him. He lies there in the dark, afraid to move, afraid to fall back asleep. By the time dawn arrives, he's exhausted.

During the day, he moves through the house like a ghost. Certain sounds-a car door slamming, an unexpected knock-send him into an acute panic. His breathing becomes shallow, his vision narrows, and for several minutes he's no longer in his comfortable home in Melbourne; he's back in that compound, uncertain and terrified. Catherine has learned to warn him before she does anything that might startle him, but she can't control the outside world.

He avoids leaving the house as much as possible. The thought of being in unfamiliar spaces, of being unable to quickly identify exits or escape routes, fills him with a dread so profound that he often talks himself out of going to the grocery store. He's lost weight. Catherine worries constantly.

What troubles Marcus most is the guilt. He feels guilty for what his trauma has done to Catherine, for the burden he's placed on their marriage. He feels guilty that he can no longer work, that he's become dependent on her emotionally and financially. He feels guilty for surviving when he knows others didn't. These thoughts circle endlessly, particularly in those dark hours before dawn.

When he speaks about his experience now, his voice is flat, almost dissociated. He describes events as though they happened to someone else. Yet his body betrays him constantly-the trembling hands, the rapid breathing, the way his eyes dart toward exits whenever he's in an unfamiliar room.

Marcus wants his life back. He wants to hold a camera again without feeling like he's lost his mind. But the path back feels impossibly distant, obscured by fear and exhaustion and a pervasive sense that the world is fundamentally unsafe.
